questions.stem: A maternity service finds that women from one cultural community report feeling ignored during labour and are less likely to ask questions. Which leadership response best reflects respectful maternity care?

options.text: Meet with women and community representatives, examine care experiences and redesign communication and consent practices with measurable standards.
Provide staff with a reminder to be polite.
Ask families to raise concerns after discharge.
Use the same communication approach for all women to avoid differences.

questions.rationale: Respectful maternity care requires dignity, informed choice and freedom from discrimination. Leaders should use patient experience data and co-design practical improvements rather than rely on reminders alone.

questions.stem: Junior staff hesitate to activate an obstetric emergency call because they fear criticism if the situation proves less serious than expected. What should the nurse leader do?

options.text: Require medical approval before any activation.
Clarify escalation criteria, reinforce that clinical concern is a valid trigger, use simulation and provide supportive debriefing.
Reduce the number of emergency drills.
Ask junior nurses to escalate only through senior midwives.

questions.rationale: Psychological safety supports early escalation. Clear criteria, simulation and non-punitive debriefing help staff act promptly while preserving accountability.

questions.stem: Which activity best demonstrates clinical governance in maternity services?

options.text: Reliance on individual clinical judgement only.
Policies, credentialing, audit, incident review and outcome monitoring linked to leadership action.

questions.rationale: Clinical governance provides structured oversight through policy, competence assurance, audit, review and monitoring.

questions.stem: A unit performs regular emergency drills, but response times remain inconsistent. What should leaders examine next?

options.text: Only the number of staff who attended.
Whether the drill scenario was realistic enough.
Role clarity, equipment availability, workflow and whether learning is transferred into real practice.

questions.rationale: Simulation is useful only when system factors and translation into practice are evaluated.

questions.stem: A woman reports feeling coerced into a procedure during labour. What is the most appropriate leadership response?

options.text: Review the incident respectfully, examine consent and communication processes, support the woman and address system and staff learning.
Explain that emergency care sometimes requires rapid decisions.
Assume the procedure was justified and take no action.
Refer the issue only to legal services.

questions.rationale: Respectful care includes informed choice and freedom from mistreatment. Leaders should review both the individual experience and the system conditions that enabled it.

questions.stem: Which outcome best indicates psychological safety within a maternity team?

options.text: Emergency calls decrease to near zero.
Staff ask questions, admit uncertainty and escalate abnormal findings without humiliation.
Near misses are discussed informally but not reported.

questions.rationale: Psychological safety is demonstrated when staff can speak up early and safely.

questions.stem: A new graduate is assigned to manage a high-risk labour without adequate supervision. Which leadership principle has been breached?

options.text: Alignment of staff competence and support with patient acuity.

questions.rationale: Safe services require that competence, staffing and supervision match clinical risk.

questions.stem: Which approach best strengthens emergency readiness for postpartum haemorrhage?

options.text: Posting the protocol on the wall.
Relying on experienced staff to lead without drills.
Regular multidisciplinary simulation, standardised equipment, role allocation and post-event review.

questions.rationale: Readiness depends on capability, equipment, role clarity and repeated practice.

questions.stem: A leader notices that respectful care standards deteriorate during high workload. What is the best action?

options.text: Review staffing, workflow and priorities so dignity, consent and communication remain reliable.
Accept reduced communication during busy periods.

questions.rationale: Respectful care is a safety standard and should not disappear under pressure.

questions.stem: Which measure would best evaluate respectful maternity care?

options.text: Patient-reported experience of dignity, communication and involvement, reviewed across different groups.

questions.rationale: Respectful care should be measured through patient experience and equity data.

questions.stem: A senior clinician publicly dismisses a junior nurse's concern about fetal deterioration. What should the service leader do?

options.text: Ignore the interaction because the senior clinician is accountable.
Ask the junior nurse to be more confident next time.
Address the behaviour, reinforce escalation expectations and ensure the patient is reviewed.
Delay action until the annual performance review.

questions.rationale: Hierarchy and humiliation undermine psychological safety and can delay care.

questions.stem: Which statement best reflects fair accountability?

options.text: Every incident should receive the same response.
Only system factors should be considered.
Leaders distinguish human error, at-risk behaviour and reckless behaviour while examining system contributors.

questions.rationale: Fair accountability balances learning with proportionate response to behaviour and context.

questions.stem: A maternity service introduces a new fetal monitoring protocol. What is needed beyond policy publication?

options.text: Training, equipment, workflow integration, competency assessment and audit.
No further action if the guideline is evidence-based.

questions.rationale: Evidence-based policy must be translated into reliable practice through implementation supports.

questions.stem: A woman with limited English is excluded from discussions because the team is busy. Which leadership standard is most relevant?
questions.rationale: Respectful care requires communication access, including interpreter use where needed.

questions.stem: Which action best develops clinical judgement in maternity emergencies?

options.text: Case review, simulation, supervised practice and reflective feedback.

questions.rationale: Judgement develops through active, supported learning and reflection.

questions.stem: A service has strong policies but repeated failures in emergency response. What does this suggest?

options.text: Policies are sufficient and staff are solely responsible.
More policies are the only solution.
There is a gap between governance documents and operational reliability.

questions.rationale: Visible leadership and implementation are needed to make policy reliable in practice.

questions.stem: A woman reports discrimination based on age and marital status. What should the leader do?

options.text: Investigate respectfully, support the woman and examine whether service practices create unequal treatment.
Treat it as a customer-service complaint only.
Advise her to make a written complaint after discharge.
Ignore the concern if clinical care was technically correct.

questions.rationale: Freedom from discrimination is part of respectful and safe maternity care.

questions.stem: Which outcome best demonstrates effective maternity leadership?

options.text: Women receive dignified care, staff escalate concerns early and emergency responses are reliable.
The unit has fewer complaints because reporting is difficult.

questions.rationale: Effective leadership combines respectful care, psychological safety and reliable clinical systems.

questions.stem: A near miss during neonatal resuscitation reveals confusion over roles. What should happen?

options.text: Blame the least experienced staff member.
Avoid discussion because no harm occurred.
Conduct a structured review, clarify roles, update drills and monitor future performance.
Add another written policy without practice.

questions.rationale: Near misses provide valuable learning and should drive practical system improvement.

questions.stem: What is the central role of a Global Nursing Professional in maternity leadership?

options.text: Delegate all quality work to managers.
Focus only on clinical outcomes, not experience.
Connect respectful practice, workforce capability, governance and system improvement.

questions.rationale: Level 3 leadership extends beyond individual care to the systems that support safe and respectful services. Section 2 - Improving Maternal and Neonatal Safety Systems

questions.stem: A maternal death review identifies delays in recognising shock, unclear escalation roles and unavailable emergency equipment. Which response best reflects systems thinking?

options.text: Redesign recognition, role allocation and equipment access, then monitor response times and outcomes.
Focus on the final nurse who documented the deterioration.
Provide a general reminder to be more careful.
Suspend one staff member and close the review.

questions.rationale: Systems thinking examines interacting clinical and organisational contributors and leads to measurable redesign.

questions.stem: Which feature is essential for a maternal early warning system to improve outcomes?

options.text: Accurate completion linked to timely escalation and response.

questions.rationale: A tool is useful only when it leads to timely clinical action.

questions.stem: A neonatal observation pathway identifies risk, but review is delayed because no receiving clinician is clearly responsible. What is the primary weakness?

options.text: The connection between recognition and response.

questions.rationale: Recognition without a reliable response pathway does not protect patients.

questions.stem: A rural facility has repeated delays transferring women with severe preeclampsia. What should leaders examine?

options.text: Whether staff can complete more documentation.
Whether women should travel earlier in pregnancy.
Referral criteria, communication channels, transport arrangements, stabilisation capacity and receiving-team coordination.

questions.rationale: Safe referral requires a complete pathway, particularly in rural settings.

questions.stem: Which review process is most appropriate after a stillbirth?

options.text: A respectful multidisciplinary review examining clinical care, communication and system factors.
Review by the final clinician only.
No review unless a complaint is made.
A discussion focused only on individual errors.

questions.rationale: Serious-event review should support learning while respecting families and staff.

questions.stem: A unit's postpartum haemorrhage trolleys differ between rooms. What is the strongest risk control?

options.text: Ask staff to memorise each trolley layout.
Standardise trolley contents and layout, label clearly and audit readiness.

questions.rationale: Standardisation reduces delay and reliance on memory during emergencies.

questions.stem: Which human factor most likely contributes to missed deterioration?
questions.rationale: Workload, fatigue and hierarchy can impair recognition and escalation.

questions.stem: A service reports that neonatal deterioration is recognised but escalation is often delayed at night. What is the best next step?

options.text: Analyse night-shift senior coverage, communication pathways and access to specialist support.

questions.rationale: The pattern suggests shift-specific system barriers requiring targeted redesign.

questions.stem: Why should serious-event reviews include frontline staff?

options.text: They understand how work is actually performed and where system pressures occur.
They can identify who is to blame.
They eliminate the need for data.

questions.rationale: Frontline insight helps explain practical workflow and latent conditions.

questions.stem: Which recommendation is least likely to prevent recurrence after an incident?

options.text: Tell staff to be more careful.

questions.rationale: General reminders are weak controls because they rely on memory and attention.

questions.stem: A maternal early warning score remains below the threshold, but the nurse is deeply concerned. What should the system permit?

options.text: No escalation until the score rises.
Review only if the woman requests it.

questions.rationale: Clinical judgement should be able to trigger review even when scores are not elevated.

questions.stem: Which measure best evaluates referral-system performance?

options.text: Time from recognition to acceptance and transfer, with maternal and neonatal outcomes.

questions.rationale: A complete measure should assess timeliness and outcomes across the referral pathway.

questions.stem: A review finds that emergency role cards improved response speed but confused new staff. What should leaders do?

options.text: Refine the cards, retrain staff and retest through simulation.

questions.rationale: Improvement should be adapted using feedback and testing.

questions.stem: Which outcome indicates a reliable deterioration system?

options.text: Abnormal trends are recognised, escalated and treated before preventable collapse.

questions.rationale: Reliability is shown by timely recognition and response.

questions.stem: A maternal near miss involves equipment that was present but difficult to locate. What type of control is most appropriate?

options.text: Redesign storage and standardise equipment placement.

questions.rationale: System redesign is stronger than reminders when equipment access is the problem.

questions.stem: Why should families be included in deterioration systems where appropriate?

options.text: They may recognise changes from baseline and provide another safety signal.

questions.rationale: Family observations can contribute to earlier recognition when taken seriously and assessed.

questions.stem: A service reviews maternal deaths but does not assign responsibility for recommendations. What is the main problem?

options.text: Recommendations may not be implemented or monitored.
The events are too rare to measure.

questions.rationale: Actions need ownership, timelines and evaluation.

questions.stem: Which action best strengthens transfer safety?

options.text: Send the patient as soon as transport arrives.
Stabilise within capability, provide concise handover, prepare equipment and confirm receiving-team acceptance.
Wait until all tests are complete.

questions.rationale: Safe transfer requires stabilisation, communication and continuity until care is accepted.

questions.stem: A review finds that women from remote communities experience longer referral delays. What should leaders do?

options.text: Report the average referral time only.
Apply the same pathway without modification.
Analyse outcomes by population and redesign services to address geographic inequity.

questions.rationale: Equity analysis should identify unequal access and outcomes across groups.

questions.stem: Which outcome best demonstrates systems improvement after a serious event?

options.text: Specific controls are implemented, response becomes more reliable and outcomes improve.

questions.rationale: Learning should result in measurable change, not documentation alone. Section 3 - Quality Improvement and Evidence Translation

questions.stem: A maternity service identifies a high rate of newborn hypothermia. What should the improvement team do first?

options.text: Define the problem using baseline data and map current care from birth through transfer.
Train all staff before understanding the process.

questions.rationale: Improvement begins by defining the problem and understanding current practice.

questions.stem: Which is an outcome measure for a newborn-warming initiative?
questions.rationale: Outcome measures describe what happened to patients.

questions.stem: Which is a process measure for the same initiative?

options.text: Percentage of newborns receiving immediate drying and skin-to-skin contact.

questions.rationale: Process measures show whether recommended care occurred.

questions.stem: Which is a balancing measure for uninterrupted skin-to-skin contact?

options.text: Maternal comfort and whether necessary newborn assessment is delayed.

questions.rationale: Balancing measures identify unintended effects.

questions.stem: A guideline on severe hypertension is published but practice does not change. What is the most likely problem?

options.text: The guideline has not been translated into practical workflow, training, equipment and documentation.
Staff do not need the guideline.

questions.rationale: Policy alone rarely changes practice without implementation supports.

questions.stem: Why are small tests of change useful?

options.text: They allow teams to learn and adapt before wider implementation.
They remove the need for measurement.

questions.rationale: Small tests reduce risk and support local learning.

questions.stem: A service improves haemorrhage response time but increases unnecessary emergency activations. What should the team do?

options.text: Ignore the increase because response is faster.
Review the balancing data and refine activation criteria.

questions.rationale: Improvement should balance benefit with unintended consequences.

questions.stem: Which data source may help identify an improvement priority?

options.text: Incident trends, audit findings, patient outcomes and staff feedback.

questions.rationale: Multiple data sources provide a more complete understanding of performance.

questions.stem: A breastfeeding-support project improves initiation rates but women from one language group still receive less support. What should leaders do?

options.text: Examine access and outcomes by population and adapt the intervention for communication needs.
Provide the same written leaflet to everyone.

questions.rationale: Equity requires examining whether improvement benefits all groups.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes evidence translation?

options.text: Turning guidance into usable pathways, education, equipment and documentation.

questions.rationale: Evidence translation embeds recommendations into everyday work.

questions.stem: A team wants to reduce delayed referral. Which process measure is most useful?

options.text: Time from recognition of risk to referral acceptance.

questions.rationale: This directly measures the targeted process.

questions.stem: A project reduces infection but increases workload to an unsustainable level. What should leaders do?

options.text: Accept the burden because infection decreased.
Review workflow and adapt the intervention before wider spread.

questions.rationale: Sustainable improvement requires acceptable balancing outcomes.

questions.stem: Which strategy best supports sustainability?

options.text: Embedding the change in workflow, equipment, documentation, audit and leadership follow-through.

questions.rationale: Sustainability requires system integration and ongoing oversight.

questions.stem: Why should patient experience be measured in maternity improvement?

options.text: Clinical outcomes alone do not show whether care was respectful, accessible and person-centred.
It is useful only after complaints.
It applies only to low-risk care.

questions.rationale: Quality includes both clinical outcomes and care experience.

questions.stem: A service introduces a new preeclampsia pathway. Which combination of measures is strongest?

options.text: Seizure rate, timely blood-pressure treatment, medication-related adverse effects and patient experience.

questions.rationale: Outcome, process, balancing and experience measures provide a complete view.

questions.stem: A pilot works well in a tertiary hospital. What should happen before implementing it in a rural service?

options.text: Assess local resources, referral capacity and workflow, then adapt while preserving core safety goals.

questions.rationale: Evidence should be adapted to local context and resources.

questions.stem: Which result best demonstrates sustainable improvement?

options.text: Improved outcomes maintained over time across different settings and populations.

questions.rationale: Sustainability and equity require continued benefit over time.

questions.stem: A process map shows repeated delays while staff search for emergency medicines. What is the strongest intervention?

options.text: Redesign storage, standardise locations and monitor availability.
Ask staff to memorise alternative locations.

questions.rationale: System redesign is more reliable than education alone.

questions.stem: Which action best supports frontline ownership of change?

options.text: Design the intervention without clinical staff.
Announce the final solution after implementation.
Involve staff in mapping, testing and refining the new process.

questions.rationale: Frontline involvement improves usability and adoption.

questions.stem: Which outcome best reflects successful quality improvement?

options.text: The targeted harm decreases, care processes become reliable and unintended effects remain acceptable across groups.

questions.rationale: Successful improvement produces measurable, sustainable and equitable benefit. Section 4 - Digital Maternity Care and Global Maternal-Newborn Health

questions.stem: A shared electronic maternity record shows that a woman has no drug allergies, but she reports a severe allergy. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Verify the history, update the record and communicate the discrepancy before treatment.
Ask the woman to wait until records are transferred.

questions.rationale: Digital records may be incomplete; critical information must be verified.

questions.stem: What is automation bias in maternity care?

options.text: Over-trusting an electronic score or interpretation despite concerning clinical findings.

questions.rationale: Automation bias occurs when technology is trusted more than direct assessment and judgement.

questions.stem: A fetal-monitoring system reports a reassuring status, but the nurse identifies recurrent concerning decelerations. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Wait for the software to change.
Use clinical judgement, verify the tracing and escalate appropriately.

questions.rationale: Technology supports but does not replace professional assessment.

questions.stem: A telehealth antenatal service is introduced for rural women. What is essential for safety?

options.text: Clear escalation pathways, local assessment options and alternatives for women without reliable internet.

questions.rationale: Remote care requires escalation pathways and attention to digital exclusion.

questions.stem: Which risk is most associated with copied electronic maternity notes?

options.text: Outdated or incorrect information being carried forward.

questions.rationale: Copied notes may create false confidence if information is outdated.

questions.stem: A service uses remote blood-pressure monitoring for high-risk pregnancy. Which design feature is most important?

options.text: A clear response pathway for abnormal readings.

questions.rationale: Monitoring has value only when abnormal results lead to timely action.

questions.stem: What is alert fatigue?

options.text: A single critical alert prompts action.
Clinicians become desensitised because alerts are excessive or frequently irrelevant.

questions.rationale: Excessive alerts can reduce attention to important warnings.

questions.stem: A woman lacks digital access for telehealth follow-up. What should the service do?

options.text: Ask her family to purchase a device.
Delay care until internet access improves.
Provide telephone, community or face-to-face alternatives.

questions.rationale: Equitable services require alternatives for people without digital access.

questions.stem: Which action best protects privacy in digital maternity care?

options.text: Use secure systems, legitimate access and careful communication.

questions.rationale: Digital convenience does not reduce confidentiality obligations.

questions.stem: A remote monitoring platform fails during a high-risk pregnancy review. What should be available?

options.text: A tested downtime and backup communication process.

questions.rationale: Downtime planning is essential for continuity and safety.

questions.stem: Which outcome best indicates equitable digital care?

options.text: High uptake among women with smartphones.
Improved access and outcomes without excluding rural, low-income or digitally limited families.

questions.rationale: Equity means benefits are shared across different populations.

questions.stem: A predictive tool repeatedly underestimates risk in one population. What should leaders do?

options.text: Review data quality, model performance and potential bias before further use.

questions.rationale: Digital tools should be evaluated for accuracy and equity across populations.

questions.stem: Why is integrated maternity care important?

options.text: It coordinates antenatal, birth, postnatal, neonatal and community services, reducing fragmented care.
It removes the need for referral.
It applies only to high-risk women.

questions.rationale: Coordination across services supports continuity and timely care.

questions.stem: A regional service adapts an international maternal-emergency pathway. What should guide adaptation?

options.text: Local disease patterns, workforce, resources, referral capacity and community needs.
A requirement to copy every step exactly.

questions.rationale: Global evidence should be adapted to local context while preserving core safety principles.

questions.stem: Which statement best reflects global maternal-newborn improvement?

options.text: One solution should be used everywhere.
Shared evidence and learning should be adapted to local resources and inequities.
Technology is the main determinant of outcomes.

questions.rationale: Global collaboration is most effective when adapted respectfully to local conditions.

questions.stem: A telehealth programme improves attendance but women report less opportunity to discuss sensitive issues. What should leaders do?

options.text: Ignore the concern because attendance improved.
Review privacy, communication and patient experience, and adapt the model.

questions.rationale: Digital improvement should consider experience and unintended effects.

questions.stem: Which measure best evaluates digital maternity equity?

options.text: Access and outcomes by geography, language, income and digital capability.

questions.rationale: Equity requires disaggregated access and outcome data.

questions.stem: A rural service lacks specialist neonatal support. Which innovation may help?

options.text: Remote specialist consultation combined with local stabilisation protocols and backup communication.

questions.rationale: Remote support can extend expertise when integrated with local capability and contingency planning.

questions.stem: Which action best reflects responsible use of fetal-monitoring technology?

options.text: Ignore patient symptoms if the tracing appears normal.
Verify digital information against direct assessment and escalate concerning findings.

questions.rationale: Technology should augment, not replace, professional judgement.

questions.stem: Which outcome best reflects the Level 3 Global Nursing Professional role?

options.text: Use digital tools critically, strengthen integrated care and adapt global evidence to improve equitable outcomes.

questions.rationale: Level 3 practice combines leadership, technology, integration, equity and global learning.
